newsitem.title: INDONESIA: RTZ-CRA unit concerned over Indonesian wage hikes.
newsitem.headline: RTZ-CRA unit concerned over Indonesian wage hikes.

text.p: The Indonesian unit of mining group RTZ-CRA said on Thursday rising labour costs could blunt the country's booming mining sector.

"Indonesia faces the risk of losing its competitive advantage unless future wage increases are coupled with productivity improvements," RTZ-CRA Indonesia president Michael Noakes told a regional mining conference in Jakarta.
He said recent negotiations at several mines suggest little or no recognition of the need to link wages with productivity.
As a consequence, new mining operations will need to carefully examine their employee levels to ensure they are sustainable over the long term, he said.
RTZ-CRA Indonesia jointly owns 50-percent of PT Kaltim Prima Coal, which operates the largest coal mine in Indonesia, and has a 90-percent stake in gold miner PT Kelian Equatorial Mining.

Noakes also said that experience has shown that many of the challenges facing the industry were not technical in nature and that the sector's desire to seek "engineering solutions to community and social issues is often misplaced".
"The ability to be able to understand local concerns and respond pro-actively will be a mark of successful companies in the future," he said.

The mining town of Timika in eastern Irian Jaya province was rocked by rampaging tribesmen last March in what was seen as a release of pent-up anger against Freeport Indonesia, which operates one of the world's largest copper-gold mines in Irian.
Irianese had claimed that Freeport, 82 percent owned by Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc, favoured immigrants from nearby islands over locals when it came to jobs.
RTZ-CRA has a 12 percent stake in Freeport McMoRan and will form a new company in Indonesia by the end of the year to hold its joint venture interests in the Freeport mine in Irian Jaya.
Noakes said the local mining industry was also likely to face increased competition for land.

"There are indications that the mining industry in Indonesia will be subjected increasingly to competing with other land users. There is a need for greater clarity as to how these competing claims are to be resolved," he said.
